purpose: Expand Safety and drug-interaction coverage using official EMA/HMPC and WHO sources without duplicating the dedicated Hypericum and Ginkgo safety Gold Cases.
governance_note: This is claim-level corpus coverage. Reuse of an authoritative source already present for a different domain is permitted only when the safety claim and locator are distinct. No Gold Case truth or production safety rule is changed.

records.safety_effect: Ivy leaf medicines must not be given to children under 2 years because cough medicines can worsen respiratory symptoms at this age.

records.population_or_drug: people hypersensitive to ivy or Araliaceae
records.safety_effect: Ivy leaf medicines must not be taken by people hypersensitive to ivy leaf or other plants of the Araliaceae family.

records.population_or_drug: progressive systemic disorders, autoimmune disease, immunodeficiency, immunosuppression, white-blood-cell disorders
records.locator: Final EU herbal monograph, section 4.4, p. 5/7
records.safety_effect: Well-established oral use is not recommended in progressive systemic disorders, autoimmune diseases, immunodeficiencies, immunosuppression, or diseases of the white blood cell system.

records.locator: EMA public summary, Risks section; final monograph section 4.4
records.safety_effect: Serious allergic reactions including asthma and anaphylactic shock have been reported, particularly in atopic patients.

records.population_or_drug: renal-transplant patients taking high oral doses for prolonged periods
records.locator: Final EU herbal monograph, section 4.5, p. 12/13
records.safety_effect: For oral use in renal-transplant patients taking high dosages for about two months, interactions based on CYP450 effects have been reported.

records.locator: Final EU herbal monograph, section 4.8, p. 12/13
records.safety_effect: Hypersensitivity reactions, including severe allergic reactions, have been reported with Matricaria flower preparations.

records.source_reference: WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Volume 1 — Radix Glycyrrhizae
records.botanical_name: Glycyrrhiza glabra L. and related official Glycyrrhiza species
records.population_or_drug: hypertension, cholestatic disorders, cirrhosis, hypokalaemia, chronic renal insufficiency, pregnancy
records.safety_effect: WHO lists hypertension, cholestatic disorders or cirrhosis, hypokalaemia, chronic renal insufficiency, and pregnancy as contraindications.

records.source_reference: WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Volume 1 — Radix Glycyrrhizae
records.botanical_name: Glycyrrhiza glabra L. and related official Glycyrrhiza species
records.population_or_drug: thiazide/loop diuretics, cardiac glycosides, antihypertensives, spironolactone, amiloride
records.safety_effect: Because liquorice increases potassium loss, WHO advises against prolonged use with thiazide or loop diuretics and cardiac glycosides; it may reduce antihypertensive effectiveness and should not be combined with spironolactone or amiloride.

records.source_reference: WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Volume 2 — Cortex Frangulae
records.botanical_name: Frangula alnus Mill. / Rhamnus frangula L.
records.population_or_drug: intestinal obstruction/inflammatory bowel disease; pregnancy; lactation; children under 12
records.safety_effect: WHO contraindicates Cortex Frangulae in several obstructive or inflammatory gastrointestinal conditions, pregnancy, lactation, and children under 12 years.

records.source_reference: WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Volume 2 — Cortex Frangulae
records.botanical_name: Frangula alnus Mill. / Rhamnus frangula L.
records.population_or_drug: cardiac glycosides, diuretics, corticosteroids, liquorice root
records.safety_effect: Chronic stimulant-laxative use can cause fluid and potassium loss; cardiac or neuromuscular dysfunction may be aggravated with cardiotonic glycosides, diuretics, corticosteroids, or liquorice root.

records.source_reference: WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Volume 1 — Bulbus Allii Sativi
records.locator: Bulbus Allii Sativi, Warnings and Drug interactions, p. 25
records.safety_effect: WHO warns that large amounts of garlic may increase postoperative bleeding risk and that garlic supplements may increase bleeding time in patients taking warfarin.

records.population_or_drug: users developing symptoms suggestive of liver injury
records.safety_effect: HMPC considered a potential connection between black cohosh products and hepatotoxicity and advised patients to stop use and seek medical care if symptoms suggestive of liver injury develop.
